summary: נְאֻם is an utterance, and in scripture nearly always Yahweh's: נְאֻם יַהְוֶה, “the utterance of Yahweh”, set by a prophet at the end, in the middle or at the head of a saying to mark the words as Yahweh's own, as in “Behold, days are coming, the utterance of Yahweh, when I will cut a new covenant” (Jer 31:31). Of its 376 uses 365 name Yahweh as the speaker, most of them in Jeremiah and Ezekiel; the other eleven are the inspired sayings of Balaam and David and the saying of Agur, the counterfeit oracle that transgression speaks in the wicked man's heart (Psa 36:2), and the false prophets who “take their tongue and utter an utterance” (Jer 23:31), the one use of the verb נָאַם. Where אָמַר “say” is said of anyone and introduces speech, נְאֻם stands outside the sentence as a claim that the speaker is Yahweh, so it is used of a man only when he speaks what God has given him; the New Testament renders it “says the Lord” (λέγει κύριος, Heb 8:8–10; Act 15:17).

words.summary: Always in the construct, followed by the speaker: “utterance of …”. It is a noun, not a verb, so it needs no subject and stands outside the syntax of the saying it marks, often breaking into the middle of a sentence (Jer 31:31; Hag 2:4).

senses.definition: נְאֻם יַהְוֶה: what a prophet speaks is declared to be Yahweh's own utterance, with Yahweh speaking in the first person on either side of it. It may close the saying, stand within it between clauses, or head it. The speaker is named as יַהְוֶה (about 268 times), אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה “the Lord Yahweh” (92, 81 of them in Ezekiel), יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת “Yahweh of armies”, הָאָדוֹן יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת “the Lord, Yahweh of armies” (Isa 1:24; 19:4), or הַמֶּלֶךְ יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת שְׁמוֹ “the King, Yahweh of armies is his name” (Jer 46:18; 48:15; 51:57).

evidence.note: “They have dealt treacherously with me, the house of Israel and the house of Judah, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה”: closing the saying; “me” is Yahweh, who is named in the formula.
הִנֵּה יָמִים בָּאִים נְאֻם יַהְוֶה וְכָרַתִּי ... בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה: within the saying, between “days are coming” and “I will cut a new covenant”. Hebrews renders it λέγει κύριος (Heb 8:8).
Three times in one verse: “be strong, Zerubbabel, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה, and be strong, Joshua … and be strong, all people of the land, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה, and work, for I am with you, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת”.
At the head of a saying: “The burden of the word of Yahweh concerning Israel. נְאֻם יַהְוֶה, who stretches out the heavens and founds the earth and forms the spirit of man within him.”
The man of God to Eli, opening and resuming: לָכֵן נְאֻם יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אָמוֹר אָמַרְתִּי ... וְעַתָּה נְאֻם יַהְוֶה: “those who honour me I will honour”.
לָכֵן נְאֻם הָאָדוֹן יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת אֲבִיר יִשְׂרָאֵל: the fullest title, at the head of the saying.
נְאֻם הַמֶּלֶךְ יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת שְׁמוֹ, “the utterance of the King, Yahweh of armies is his name”; also Jer 48:15; 51:57.
נְאֻם אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה inside the sentence: “the nations will know that I am Yahweh, the utterance of the Lord Yahweh, when I am sanctified in you before their eyes”.
נְאֻם אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהֵי הַצְּבָאוֹת.
“My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה.”
הֲלוֹא כֹה דְבָרִי כָּאֵשׁ נְאֻם יַהְוֶה: “is not my word like fire, the utterance of Yahweh, and like a hammer that breaks the rock?”
Isaiah's word on Sennacherib: “to this city he shall not come, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה”; the same in Isa 37:34.
Huldah's word to Josiah: “I also have heard, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה”; the same in 2Ch 34:27, the word's one use in Chronicles.
נְאֻם יַהְוֶה עֹשֶׂה זֹּאת, “the utterance of Yahweh, who does this”; James renders it λέγει κύριος ὁ ποιῶν ταῦτα (Act 15:17).
The council at Jerusalem quotes Amo 9:11–12 with its formula: λέγει κύριος ὁ ποιῶν ταῦτα πάντα.
Jer 31:31–33 quoted with each נְאֻם יַהְוֶה kept as λέγει κύριος, three times.

senses.definition: After an oath in Yahweh's mouth: חַי־אָנִי “as I live” or בִּי נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי “by myself I have sworn”, followed by נְאֻם יַהְוֶה. Having no one greater to swear by, he swears by his own life and names himself as the one swearing.

evidence.note: The word's first use: בִּי נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי נְאֻם יַהְוֶה, “by myself I have sworn, the utterance of Yahweh”, to Abraham after the binding of Isaac.
חַי־אָנִי נְאֻם יַהְוֶה: the oath that the generation that would not go up would die in the wilderness.
Gen 22:16–17 expounded: “since he had no one greater to swear by, he swore by himself, saying, Surely blessing I will bless you”.
חַי־אָנִי נְאֻם יַהְוֶה: Zion shall put on her gathered children like jewels.
חַי־אָנִי נְאֻם אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה: “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live”.
בִּי נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי נְאֻם יַהְוֶה: the king's house shall become a ruin; also Jer 49:13.
חַי־אָנִי נְאֻם יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל: Moab shall be like Sodom.
“As I live, says the Lord (ζῶ ἐγώ, λέγει κύριος), to me every knee shall bow”: the oath-formula of Isa 49:18 and its like, joined to Isa 45:23.

senses.gloss: the utterance of Yahweh to my lord
senses.definition: Once, at the head of a psalm, the utterance has an addressee: נְאֻם יַהְוֶה לַאדֹנִי, “the utterance of Yahweh to my lord”. David reports, as a prophet, what Yahweh says to another whom David calls his lord.

evidence.note: לְדָוִד מִזְמוֹר נְאֻם יַהְוֶה לַאדֹנִי שֵׁב לִימִינִי: “Of David, a psalm. The utterance of Yahweh to my lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”
Jesus: David speaks the verse ἐν πνεύματι, “in spirit”; the formula becomes εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου.
“David himself said in the holy spirit.”
Peter: David did not ascend; the words are of Jesus, whom “God has made both lord and Christ”.
Said to the son and to no angel.

senses.gloss: claimed by prophets Yahweh did not send
senses.definition: Because the formula claims that Yahweh is the speaker, saying it of words he has not spoken is lying in his name. Ezekiel and Jeremiah condemn prophets who say נְאֻם יַהְוֶה of their own visions.

evidence.note: חָזוּ שָׁוְא וְקֶסֶם כָּזָב הָאֹמְרִים נְאֻם יַהְוֶה: “they have seen falsehood and lying divination, who say ‘the utterance of Yahweh’, and Yahweh has not sent them”.
וְאֹמְרִים נְאֻם יַהְוֶה וַאֲנִי לֹא דִבַּרְתִּי: “and you say ‘the utterance of Yahweh’, though I have not spoken”.
“Behold, I am against the prophets, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה, who take their tongue וַיִּנְאֲמוּ נְאֻם”: who utter an utterance of their own, with the noun and its verb together.
“Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה … and I did not send them nor command them.”

senses.gloss: the utterance of a man speaking for God
senses.definition: Of a man, only where he speaks what God has given him. Balaam's last two oracles open “the utterance of Balaam son of Beor, the utterance of the man whose eye is opened, the utterance of one who hears the sayings of God”, after the spirit of God came on him; David's last words open “the utterance of David son of Jesse”, and go on “the spirit of Yahweh spoke by me, and his word was on my tongue”; Agur's words are called a burden (מַשָּׂא) and “the utterance of the man”. The man is named, but the saying is God's.

evidence.note: נְאֻם בִּלְעָם בְּנוֹ בְעֹר וּנְאֻם הַגֶּבֶר שְׁתֻם הָעָיִן נְאֻם שֹׁמֵעַ אִמְרֵי־אֵל: his utterance is that of one who hears the sayings of God and sees the vision of the Almighty.
“And the spirit of God came upon him”: the verse before the first נְאֻם בִּלְעָם.
The same opening repeated, adding “who knows the knowledge of the Most High”.
וְאֵלֶּה דִּבְרֵי דָוִד הָאַחֲרֹנִים נְאֻם דָּוִד בֶּן־יִשַׁי וּנְאֻם הַגֶּבֶר הֻקַם עָל מְשִׁיחַ אֱלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב.
רוּחַ יַהְוֶה דִּבֶּר־בִּי וּמִלָּתוֹ עַל־לְשׁוֹנִי: David's utterance is the spirit of Yahweh speaking by him.

דִּבְרֵי אָגוּר בִּן־יָקֶה הַמַּשָּׂא נְאֻם הַגֶּבֶר לְאִיתִיאֵל: “the words of Agur son of Jakeh, the burden: the utterance of the man to Ithiel”. The verse does not say how Agur received it; “burden” is the prophets' word for a message from Yahweh (Zec 12:1).

senses.definition: Once transgression itself is the speaker: it gives the wicked man its oracle within his heart, a mock of נְאֻם יַהְוֶה, and he listens, so that there is no dread of God before his eyes.

evidence.note: נְאֻם־פֶּשַׁע לָרָשָׁע בְּקֶרֶב לִבִּי אֵין־פַּחַד אֱלֹהִים לְנֶגֶד עֵינָיו: “the utterance of transgression to the wicked is within my heart; there is no dread of God before his eyes”.
Paul quotes the verse's second half among the scriptures that show all under sin: “there is no fear of God before their eyes”.
Jer 31:31–33: each נְאֻם יַהְוֶה is λέγει κύριος.
Jer 31:33 again: μετὰ τὰς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας, λέγει κύριος.
Amo 9:12: λέγει κύριος ὁ ποιῶν ταῦτα πάντα.
ζῶ ἐγώ, λέγει κύριος: the oath חַי־אָנִי נְאֻם יַהְוֶה.
λέγει for נְאֻם in Yahweh's oath; the commonest rendering, about 246 times.
λέγει, as Act 15:17 has it.
φησὶν, where Hebrews has λέγει; also at Jer 31:32 and 31:33.
φησὶν for Balaam's נְאֻם.
φησὶν for “the utterance of transgression”.
Psa 110:1: εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου for נְאֻם יַהְוֶה לַאדֹנִי.
εἶπεν, as the gospels and Acts quote it.

parallels.note: “Say”: the verb of saying beside the noun of utterance. כֹּה אָמַר opens a saying, נְאֻם marks it within or at its close, and אָמַר יַהְוֶה may close it.

evidence.note: כֹּה אָמַר יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת שׁוּבוּ אֵלַי נְאֻם יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת וְאָשׁוּב אֲלֵיכֶם אָמַר יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת: all three in one verse.
כֹּה אָמַר אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה at the head, נְאֻם אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה at the close.
“I have loved you, אָמַר יַהְוֶה … was not Esau Jacob's brother? נְאֻם יַהְוֶה.”
וַיֹּאמַר נְאֻם בִּלְעָם: “and he said: the utterance of Balaam”.

parallels.note: “Word”: the utterance is his word, and the words of David and Agur are headed by both.

evidence.note: דִּבְרֵי דָוִד ... נְאֻם דָּוִד.
דִּבְרֵי אָגוּר ... נְאֻם הַגֶּבֶר.
“He who has my word, let him speak my word faithfully … is not my word like fire? נְאֻם יַהְוֶה.”
Twice נְאֻם יַהְוֶה, then “cast him into the plot כִּדְבַר יַהְוֶה”.

parallels.note: “Burden”, the message laid on a prophet, heading a saying beside נְאֻם.
“Saying”: Balaam's utterance is that of one who hears אִמְרֵי־אֵל, “the sayings of God”.

opposites.note: “Their own heart”: the prophets Yahweh did not send speak “a vision of their own heart, not from the mouth of Yahweh”, and yet say נְאֻם יַהְוֶה.

evidence.note: חֲזוֹן לִבָּם יְדַבֵּרוּ לֹא מִפִּי יַהְוֶה.
לִנְבִיאֵי מִלִּבָּם, “to the prophets out of their own heart”, before the charge of 13:6–7.
“Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה.”

phrases.gloss: the utterance of the Lord Yahweh (Ezekiel's usual form)

evidence.note: “I have no pleasure in the death of the one who dies, נְאֻם אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה; so turn and live.”

phrases.gloss: the utterance of Yahweh of armies

evidence.note: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, against the man who is my fellow, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת; strike the shepherd and the flock will scatter”: quoted by Jesus in Mat 26:31.

phrases.gloss: as I live, the utterance of Yahweh: Yahweh's oath
by myself I have sworn, the utterance of Yahweh
behold, days are coming, the utterance of Yahweh: announcing what Yahweh will do

evidence.note: “… when I will raise up for David a righteous branch, and he shall reign as king.”

phrases.gloss: in that day, the utterance of Yahweh

evidence.note: “In that day, נְאֻם יַהְוֶה, you will call me ‘my husband’ and no longer call me ‘my Baal’.”

words.summary: Used once, made from the noun and joined to it: the false prophets “utter an utterance”. One use is little for a verb, but the noun beside it fixes what it means: to give out one's own words in the form of Yahweh's.

stems.gloss: utter an utterance, speak as though Yahweh spoke

senses.definition: To put out a saying as an utterance of Yahweh. Its one use is of prophets who “take their tongue”, their own speech, and make an utterance of it; Yahweh says in the next verse that he did not send them.

evidence.note: הִנְנִי עַל־הַנְּבִיאִם נְאֻם יַהְוֶה הַלֹּקְחִים לְשׁוֹנָם וַיִּנְאֲמוּ נְאֻם: “Behold, I am against the prophets, the utterance of Yahweh, who take their tongue and utter an utterance.”
The verse before: they steal Yahweh's words, each from his neighbour.
“I did not send them nor command them.”

cognates.gloss: utter a moaning cry (of an owl, and of a man)
cognates.note: Not found as its own article in the vendored Lane; it is given as the synonym of نَأَجَ “it (an owl) uttered a moaning cry, … and in like manner a man”. A low voiced sound, not a declaration: if it is the same root, Hebrew has narrowed it to a solemn utterance. Too slight to rest the meaning on.

evidence.locator: p. 2751, root نأج, نَأَجَ (n39116), section A2
evidence.note: “نَأَجَ … It (an owl) uttered a moaning cry; or hooted; syn. نَأَمَ: (K:) and in like manner a man. (TA.)”

doctrine.statement: The prophets set נְאֻם יַהְוֶה inside their sayings 365 times, with Yahweh speaking as “I” on either side of it (Jer 31:31–34; Hag 2:4): the words are spoken by a man, and the man says they are Yahweh's utterance. Of a man the word is used only where God has given the words: the spirit of God came on Balaam before “the utterance of Balaam” (Num 24:2–4), and David, at “the utterance of David”, says “the spirit of Yahweh spoke by me, and his word was on my tongue” (2Sa 23:1–2). The claim can be false: Yahweh is against the prophets “who say, ‘the utterance of Yahweh’, though I have not spoken” (Ezk 13:6–7), who “take their tongue and utter an utterance”, whom he did not send (Jer 23:31–32), speaking a vision of their own heart (Jer 23:16). What Yahweh utters he does: “the word that I speak will be done, נְאֻם אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה” (Ezk 12:25, 28). The New Testament reads the formula the same way: Hebrews keeps it as “says the Lord” (Heb 8:8–10), and says God spoke in the prophets (Heb 1:1); Peter, that no prophecy came by the will of man, but men spoke from God carried by holy spirit (2Pe 1:21). So the prophets' utterance is God's word given by his spirit, his power working in a man, and not the man's own; and to claim it for one's own words is to lie in his name.

Psalm 110 opens נְאֻם יַהְוֶה לַאדֹנִי, “the utterance of Yahweh to my lord”, with the word the prophets use for Yahweh's own speech: David reports as a prophet what Yahweh says, and Jesus says David spoke it “in spirit” (Mat 22:43), “in the holy spirit” (Mrk 12:36). The utterance is Yahweh's and it is spoken to another, whom David calls his lord: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet” (Psa 110:1). The speaker and the one spoken to are two. Peter says that David did not ascend into the heavens, that the words are of Jesus, and that God has made him both lord and Christ (Act 2:34–36); Hebrews, that they were said to the son and to no angel (Heb 1:13). So the one God, Yahweh, speaks, and the one he addresses is David's son, a man whom God has raised and made lord.

The word first appears in Yahweh's oath to Abraham after the binding of Isaac: “by myself I have sworn, the utterance of Yahweh, … I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply your seed” (Gen 22:16–17). He swears by himself, or by his own life (“as I live, the utterance of Yahweh”, Num 14:28; Isa 49:18; Ezk 33:11). Hebrews explains: having no one greater to swear by, he swore by himself, so that by two unchangeable things, the promise and the oath, in which God cannot lie, those who have fled for refuge may hold fast the hope set before them (Heb 6:13–18). The promise to Abraham stands on the utterance of Yahweh under oath, and cannot fail.

note:
Root: נאמ, the key the words are filed under and the database's root for them; no other entry has it. The noun is taken as the base and the verb, used once, as made from it.

Counts, from the pointed text: 376 tokens of the noun. 365 name Yahweh as speaker: יַהְוֶה alone about 268, אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה 92 (Ezekiel 81, Amos 5, Jeremiah 4, Isaiah 2), הָאָדוֹן יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת 2 (Isa 1:24; 19:4), הַמֶּלֶךְ יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת שְׁמוֹ 3 (Jer 46:18; 48:15; 51:57); these include the two in Ezk 13:6–7 where false prophets say it. The other 11: Balaam 6 (Num 24:3 ×2, 4, 15 ×2, 16), David 2 (2Sa 23:1), Agur 1 (Pro 30:1), transgression 1 (Psa 36:2), and the cognate object of Jer 23:31. By book: Jeremiah 176, Ezekiel 85, Isaiah 25, Amos 21, Zechariah 20, Haggai 12, Numbers 7, Zephaniah 5, Hosea 4, 2 Kings 4; once or twice in Gen, 1Sa, 2Sa, Joel, Obadiah, Micah, Nahum, Malachi, Psalms, Proverbs, 2 Chronicles. Not in Daniel, Jonah, Habakkuk, or the rest of the Writings. The verse numbers are the Hebrew text's (Psa 36:2 is English 36:1; Hos 2:15, 18, 23 are English 2:13, 16, 21).

No Aramaic word: Biblical Aramaic has no נאם, and the brief found no Peshitta root. The Peshitta's rendering of λέγει κύριος in Heb 8:8–10 was not checked.

Greek: the Septuagint's πιστός at 2Sa 23:1 (×2) reads the letters as נֶאֱמָן, and its νυστάζοντας at Jer 23:31 reads the verb as נוּם “slumber”; neither is recorded, having no bearing on the New Testament's words. λέγω, φημί and εἶπον are common words, given only as the bridge; λέγει κύριος in Hebrews 8 differs from the Septuagint's φησὶν κύριος at Jer 31:31–33.

The New Testament quotes other verses that carry the formula without rendering it: Zec 13:7 (Mat 26:31), Isa 59:20 (Rom 11:26), Isa 52:5 (Rom 2:24). Rom 14:11 joins ζῶ ἐγώ, λέγει κύριος to Isa 45:23, which has בִּי נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי but not נְאֻם; it is cited for the formula of Isa 49:18 and the other חַי־אָנִי oaths, which is a judgment for the reviewer.

Psa 110:1 is treated as in adon.json (sense `davids-lord` there and its doctrine `yahweh-and-davids-lord`), with “the utterance of Yahweh to my lord”.

Leads not followed: (a) Lane has no article for نأم in the vendored file (the entries keyed نءم at p. 3040 are of نوم “sleep”), so the Arabic rests on one mention under نأج; the Arabic noun نَئِيم “groaning” and the root's own article in the Tāj al-ʿArūs were not checked. (b) Later Hebrew נוּם / נָאַם “to speak, say” (Tosefta Ohalot 4:14, as Jastrow gives it, s.v. נוּם) is Hebrew, not a cognate language, and was not recorded; whether Jewish Aramaic has the verb was not checked in CAL. (c) No Akkadian, Ugaritic, Phoenician, Ge'ez or South Arabian cognate was found in the vendored sources; the Oracc candidates of shape n-m (inimmû “word” and others) do not have the ʾ and were not taken. DULAT and the Sabaic Dictionary were not consulted.
